title: A world of unfamiliar faces
text: Some people cannot recognise faces — not a quirk of memory but a condition called prosopagnosia, which affects an estimated one person in fifty in its milder {{1}}. Ask a sufferer to describe a face and they will list its {{2}} — glasses, a beard, a mole — yet five minutes later the same face is a stranger's. Voices, hairstyles and walking styles {{3}} the gap, which is why sufferers manage most encounters, and why the condition so often goes undiagnosed: from outside, it looks like rudeness. The condition has {{4}} neuroscience's map of the brain: studies show a dedicated region that responds to faces specifically, and damage to it leaves other visual skills untouched. People can read expressions perfectly well and still fail to {{5}} whose face they are reading. Developmental prosopagnosia, present from birth without any injury, shows the ability is {{6}} rather than generally learned — though nobody is born knowing Grandmother, the {{7}} to learn faces seems to be set early. Sufferers develop strategies: some greet everyone warmly to hide the uncertainty; others, like the late neurologist Oliver Sacks, who had the condition himself, simply {{8}} the truth and apologise for not recognising an old friend.

gaps.explanation: 'affects an estimated one person in fifty in its milder forms' — varieties of the condition; fashions, forces and fortunes do not grade a condition.
'list its features — glasses, a beard, a mole' — the visible parts; fixture = a fitting or a sports match.
'voices and hairstyles bridge the gap' — span it; broaden would widen the gap, reversing the meaning.
'has redrawn neuroscience's map of the brain' — forced scientists to draw it again; rewind is for tape, redo is vaguer and ungrammatical with 'map' here.
'fail to tell whose face they are reading' — 'tell' here means distinguish or know; say needs the wording of a statement.
'the ability is innate rather than learned' — inborn; inert = motionless, intermittent = stopping and starting.
'the capacity to learn faces seems to be set early' — the built-in ability; caption = a text under a picture, captivity = imprisonment.
'simply admit the truth and apologise' — acknowledge it openly; the other -mit verbs share the form, not the meaning.
